reference.source: Sperling Pediatric Endocrinology / Williams Textbook of Endocrinology
clinicalPearls: The adrenal gland is the commonest site of neonatal haemorrhage, favoured by its relatively large size and rich vascularity at birth
Recognised risk factors include birth trauma, difficult or breech delivery, macrosomia, perinatal hypoxia or asphyxia, sepsis, and coagulopathy or haemorrhagic disease of the newborn
Presentation ranges from an asymptomatic incidental finding to a flank mass, anaemia, prolonged jaundice, or, if bilateral and extensive, adrenal insufficiency
It is more common on the right side and may be bilateral
Ultrasound is the first-line investigation and typically shows an evolving suprarenal mass that changes and shrinks over serial scans
The main differential of a neonatal suprarenal mass is neuroblastoma, which serial imaging and urinary catecholamine metabolites help to distinguish
Most cases resolve spontaneously with supportive care, and surgery is reserved for ongoing bleeding or diagnostic uncertainty
reference.pathophysiology: The neonatal adrenal cortex is proportionally large and highly vascular, making it vulnerable to haemorrhage when subjected to the mechanical stress of delivery, hypoxic-ischaemic injury, venous congestion, or the endothelial effects of sepsis. Impaired haemostasis, whether from coagulopathy or vitamin K-dependent haemorrhagic disease, compounds the risk. Extensive bilateral bleeding can destroy enough cortex to cause adrenal insufficiency, whereas unilateral bleeds usually resolve, often leaving residual calcification.
additionalDifferentials: Neuroblastoma, the key differential of a suprarenal mass
Renal masses such as mesoblastic nephroma or renal vein thrombosis with haemorrhage
additionalInvestigations: Serial abdominal ultrasound showing an evolving, involuting suprarenal lesion
Haematocrit and haemoglobin monitoring alongside bilirubin
Coagulation screen and sepsis evaluation where indicated
Urinary catecholamine metabolites to help exclude neuroblastoma
MRI if diagnostic uncertainty persists or to characterise a persistent mass
Assessment of adrenal function including cortisol and electrolytes if the haemorrhage is bilateral or extensive
redFlags: Signs of adrenal insufficiency such as hypotension, hypoglycaemia and hyponatraemia with bilateral haemorrhage
Ongoing haemorrhage with haemodynamic instability or a falling haematocrit
A suprarenal mass that fails to involute, raising concern for neuroblastoma
Sepsis or coagulopathy requiring urgent treatment
reference.prognosis: Generally excellent for unilateral haemorrhage, which resolves spontaneously and often leaves residual calcification; the outcome is worse with extensive bilateral disease causing adrenal insufficiency or when an underlying illness is severe.
pitfalls: Mistaking neuroblastoma for adrenal haemorrhage, or vice versa, without serial imaging and catecholamine testing
Missing adrenal insufficiency in bilateral haemorrhage
Overlooking an underlying coagulopathy or sepsis
Proceeding to surgery for a lesion that would resolve with observation
management: Manage most unilateral haemorrhages conservatively, as they resolve spontaneously
Provide supportive care with transfusion for significant anaemia and phototherapy for prolonged jaundice
Correct coagulopathy, including vitamin K for haemorrhagic disease of the newborn, and treat any underlying sepsis
Replace glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid if extensive bilateral haemorrhage causes adrenal insufficiency
Monitor with serial abdominal ultrasound to confirm involution and with urinary catecholamine metabolites to help exclude neuroblastoma
Refer for paediatric surgical or oncological assessment and MRI if a suprarenal mass fails to involute
